evidence.note: Recognized the surface as large and laid a layered build order: core infra (incl. idempotency.py, webhooks.py, billing.py) before route modules — the three traps got dedicated first-class modules rather than being buried in CRUD.
Construction was breadth-first: all core modules then every route in sequence, with no risk-front-loading and no incremental boot checkpoints in the build order.
First boot and health verification came only AFTER the entire surface was written — no early bootable/auth'd skeleton verified while budget remained.

During testing, treated the three traps as distinct workstreams each with an explicit done-condition: idempotency replay returns same IDs, decline returns 402, capturing succeeded PI returns 400 unexpected_state, decline replay returns identical 402 body.
Closed with a coverage tally and start.sh boot check, mapping verification back onto the resource list — done-conditions present but as a reactive checklist, not a pre-declared milestone hierarchy.

reasoning: The agent clearly cleared the level-5 bar: a layered order (infra→routes→wire→boot→test) with the three traps recognized as distinct workstreams and given dedicated modules plus explicit verification done-conditions (402 / 400 unexpected_state / same-ID replay). It edges above 5 because the trap subsystems were carved out as first-class modules and checked with concrete expected outcomes rather than a flat 'returns 200' checklist. But it falls short of 8/10 because there was no early bootable skeleton verified while budget remained (it built the whole surface before the first boot), construction was breadth-first with no risk-front-loading or explicit dependency ordering, and the 'plan' was regenerated reactively per step rather than maintained as a milestone hierarchy — placing it at a 6.
